examples.title: Building the Capstone AIClient: Request Handling, Retries, Rate Limits, and a Real Test
examples.context: Lesson 21's capstone brief asks for one `AIClient` class that demonstrates every requirement from Chapters 3 and 4 at once: correct request/response handling, resilient error handling, rate-limit awareness, a tested retry path, and clean class design. Lessons 17, 18, 19, and 20 each built one piece of this class in isolation. This worked example is the finished assembly — the same class, with every piece wired together the way the capstone actually asks for, plus the one mocked test the brief requires.
examples.objective: Produce a single `AIClient` class that wraps Anthropic's Messages API, retries only transient failures with real backoff, honors the API's own `retry-after` header when present, raises a specific exception when retries are exhausted, and ships with a passing mocked test proving the retry path actually works.
examples.startingInformation:
**What each chapter already established:**
- The real Messages API request/response shape (Lesson 11): `model`, `messages`, `max_tokens` in, `content`/`stop_reason`/`usage` out
- The real error shape and which status codes are worth retrying — 429 and 5xx, never 400 or 401 (Lesson 14)
- A client class centralizes shared config in `__init__` via a `requests.Session` (Lesson 17)
- Custom exceptions (`RateLimitError`, `APIError`) so callers catch specific errors instead of inspecting raw status codes (Lesson 18)
- The real rate-limit headers — `retry-after`, `anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining` — and that `retry-after` should be read, not guessed (Lesson 19)
- Mocking `session.post` with `unittest.mock` so tests are fast, free, and deterministic (Lesson 20)
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — `__init__` holds everything shared.** The API key, base URL, and a `requests.Session` with the required headers are set up once (Lesson 17) — every method below reuses `self.session` instead of rebuilding the connection and headers per call.

**Step 2 — Give errors real names.** `RateLimitError` and `APIError` (Lesson 18) are defined so callers can write `except RateLimitError:` instead of checking `resp.status_code == 429` themselves.

**Step 3 — `send_message` retries only transient failures.** The retry loop checks for `429` or `>= 500` (Lesson 14's transient category) — anything else (a `400` or `401`) raises immediately via `raise_for_status()`, because retrying a malformed request or a bad key can never succeed.

**Step 4 — Read `retry-after` instead of guessing.** When the API includes a `retry-after` header on a `429` response, the loop waits exactly that long; only when the header is missing does it fall back to the exponential-backoff guess (`2 ** attempt`) from Lesson 18's original version.

**Step 5 — Prove the retry path actually works.** `test_retries_on_rate_limit` (Lesson 20) mocks `session.post` to return a `429` first and a success second, patches `time.sleep` so the test runs instantly, and asserts the final result is the successful response — not a guess that the loop "should" work.
examples.reasoning:
The one change worth calling out versus Lesson 18's original retry loop is **Step 4**: reading `retry-after` when it's present instead of always falling back to a fixed exponential guess. Anthropic's API tells you exactly how long it wants you to wait on a 429 — ignoring that and guessing anyway risks retrying too soon (getting rate-limited again immediately) or waiting longer than necessary. Preferring the server's own number, with the guess only as a fallback when no header is sent, is strictly better information whenever it's available.

The second deliberate choice is keeping `test_retries_on_rate_limit` as a **mocked** test, never a real API call, exactly per Lesson 20's reasoning: a real call can't reliably be made to return a 429 on command, costs money, and takes real network time. The mock proves the client's own retry logic works, which is the only thing this test is actually responsible for — not whether Anthropic's servers are currently rate-limiting anyone.
examples.validation: Run both tests and confirm they pass in well under a second, with no network calls and no real API key required — that speed and determinism is itself proof the mocking (Lesson 20) was done correctly. Separately, confirm `send_message("claude-sonnet-5", [...])` against a genuinely malformed request (an empty `messages` list) raises `APIError` immediately, in a single attempt, with no retry delay — proving Step 3's "never retry a 400" rule actually holds, not just that it's written in a comment.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Retrying every non-200 response, including 400s and 401s.** This wastes two full retry cycles (with real sleep delays) on a request that will never succeed no matter how many times it's sent — Lesson 14's transient-vs-permanent distinction exists precisely to prevent this.
- **Always using the exponential-backoff guess, even when `retry-after` is present.** The API is telling you the exact right number; ignoring it in favor of a guess throws away free, accurate information.
- **Testing against the real API instead of mocking `session.post`.** A test suite that calls the live API can't reliably simulate a 429, costs money per run, and becomes flaky the moment the network has a bad day — none of which has anything to do with whether the client's own logic is correct.
- **Forgetting to patch `time.sleep` in the test.** Without it, `test_retries_on_rate_limit` genuinely pauses for real seconds during every test run — correct in behavior, but it silently makes the whole test suite slow over time as more retry tests are added.

examples.title: A Complete Tool-Calling Round Trip: get_weather, End to End
examples.context: Lesson 13 introduces each piece of tool calling separately — the `input_schema`, the `tool_use` block, the `tool_result` reply — using the same `get_weather` example throughout. What it doesn't show as one continuous trace is what actually travels back and forth across all four messages, from the first user question to Claude's final natural-language answer. This worked example runs that exact `get_weather` tool through the complete round trip, so every message's real JSON shape is visible in sequence.
examples.objective: Walk a single user question — "What's the weather in San Francisco?" — through the full tool-calling round trip: define the tool, receive Claude's `tool_use` request, actually run the lookup, send back a `tool_result`, and receive Claude's final answer.
examples.startingInformation: **What's already defined, from Lesson 13:** the `get_weather` tool's shape, using the JSON Schema keywords from Lesson 8 (`type`, `properties`, `required`) to describe its one argument, `location`. **What's new here:** the actual function behind the tool (a stand-in that returns a fixed value, standing in for a real weather API call) and the two full request bodies that go back and forth — the first message and the follow-up carrying the tool's result.
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Send the first request, with the tool definition attached.** The request body carries the user's question and the `tools` array containing `get_weather`'s full definition — Claude sees the tool is available but hasn't decided yet whether it's needed.

**Step 2 — Read Claude's response: a `tool_use` block, not a text answer.** Because answering the question requires live data Claude doesn't have, `stop_reason` comes back as `"tool_use"`, and the content block names the tool (`get_weather`), carries a unique `id`, and fills in `input` according to the schema — `{"location": "San Francisco, CA"}`.

**Step 3 — Actually run the function.** This is the one step that happens entirely in your own application code, outside any API call: read `name` and `input` off the `tool_use` block, call the real (or, here, stand-in) weather lookup, and get back a plain result — `"15 degrees Celsius, partly cloudy"`.

**Step 4 — Send the result back as a new message.** The second request repeats the full conversation history (the original user message, Claude's `tool_use` reply) and appends a new user-role message containing a `tool_result` block — critically, with `tool_use_id` set to the *exact* `id` Claude generated in Step 2, so Claude can match the result to the call that asked for it.

**Step 5 — Read Claude's final answer.** This time `stop_reason` comes back `"end_turn"`, and the content is a normal text block — Claude has read the tool's result and written a natural-language reply using it.
examples.reasoning:
The detail that matters most across this whole round trip is **`tool_use_id` matching, in Step 4**. Nothing about the JSON format would raise an error if that ID were wrong or missing — but Claude would have no way to know which of (potentially several) pending tool calls this result answers, especially in a conversation where more than one tool was called in the same turn. Carrying that ID through exactly, unchanged, from the `tool_use` block to the `tool_result` block is what keeps a multi-tool conversation from becoming ambiguous.

The second thing worth noticing: Claude genuinely never executes anything. Step 3 happens entirely outside the API, in application code the developer controls — this is why tool calling is safe to hand real actions to (sending an email, querying a production database) without worrying about a model running arbitrary code on its own.
examples.validation: Confirm `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"` on the first response and `"end_turn"` on the second — that's the signal telling your application code whether it needs to run a function and loop back, or whether the conversation turn is actually finished. Separately, confirm `tool_call["id"]` from Response 1 and `tool_use_id` in Request 2's `tool_result` block are character-for-character identical — a copy-paste mismatch here is a real, common bug and won't necessarily raise an obvious error.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Treating the first response as a final answer.** Code that reads `content[0].text` unconditionally crashes (or silently misbehaves) on a `tool_use` response, because that content block has no `text` field at all — always check `stop_reason` first.
- **Forgetting to resend the full conversation history in Request 2.** The second request isn't just the tool result in isolation — it needs the original user message and Claude's `tool_use` reply included too, so Claude has the full context to write a coherent final answer.
- **Generating a new ID instead of reusing Claude's.** `tool_use_id` must be copied exactly from the `id` Claude generated — inventing a new one breaks the link between the call and its result.
- **Assuming the model can call the function itself.** Nothing happens automatically between Response 1 and Request 2 — the actual function call (Step 3) is application code the developer must write and run.

examples.title: A Reliable Webhook Handler for Async Batch Job Completion
examples.context: Lesson 16 covers webhook basics in isolation — the event shape, signature verification, responding fast. Lesson 15 separately covers cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. A real AI application that submits batch jobs (Lesson 11's provider-API pattern applied to large async workloads) needs both working together: a webhook that reacts the moment a batch finishes, plus a pagination-based backfill for the (rare, but real) case where a webhook delivery is missed entirely. This worked example builds that combination as one small, production-shaped piece of code.
examples.objective: Write a webhook handler that verifies the event's signature, responds fast, and processes a `batch.completed` event exactly once — plus a separate backfill routine that pages through the provider's batch list endpoint to catch any batch that completed without a webhook ever arriving.
examples.startingInformation: **What's already defined, from Lesson 16:** the real event shape (`id`, `type`, `created`, `data.object`) and the signature-header pattern (`t=...,v1=...`) used to prove an event is genuine. **What's already defined, from Lesson 15:** the cursor-based `has_more`/`starting_after` pagination pattern used by AI provider list endpoints. **What's new:** combining both into one reliability story for a batch-processing feature, where silently missing a completion event means a user never finds out their job finished.
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Verify the signature before reading anything else.** The handler recomputes the HMAC signature from the raw request body, the timestamp, and the shared secret, and rejects the request immediately if it doesn't match Lesson 16's `v1=` value — nothing in the payload is trusted until this check passes.

**Step 2 — Respond `200` immediately, before doing slow work.** Per Lesson 16, the real processing (updating a database, notifying a user) is handed to a background task, and the handler returns success right away — so the provider doesn't treat a slow handler as a failed delivery and retry it.

**Step 3 — Make processing idempotent using the event's own `id`.** Webhook deliveries can arrive more than once for the same event (a provider's own retry after a slow response, a network blip). Checking whether `event["id"]` has already been processed — a quick lookup against a small "processed event IDs" store — makes a duplicate delivery a safe no-op instead of double-processing the same batch completion.

**Step 4 — Build the backfill as insurance, not the primary path.** On a schedule (hourly, say), a separate routine pages through the batch list endpoint using Lesson 15's cursor pattern (`has_more` / `starting_after`), and for any batch whose status is `completed` but whose `id` never appeared in the processed-events store, it runs the same processing logic the webhook handler would have — closing the gap for the rare case where a webhook delivery never arrived at all.
examples.reasoning:
The core decision here is treating the webhook as the **fast path** and the paginated backfill as a **safety net**, not a redundant duplicate of the same work done two different ways. Relying on webhooks alone means one lost delivery (a brief network partition, a deploy that happened to restart the server at the wrong second) silently loses an event forever, with no way to even know it happened. Relying on pagination alone (polling the list endpoint constantly) would work, but defeats the entire reason webhooks exist — near-instant notification instead of a polling delay. Running both, with the event `id` as the single source of truth for "has this already been handled," gets the speed of webhooks and the reliability of pagination without doing the real work twice.

The second deliberate choice is checking the signature (Step 1) *before* even looking at `type` or `data.object` in Step 2 or 3 — an unverified payload could claim to be a `batch.completed` event for a batch that isn't even the caller's, and nothing downstream should trust it until the signature check passes.
examples.validation: Send the same event payload and signature twice through `handle_webhook` and confirm the second call returns `200` without calling `queue_batch_processing` again — that proves Step 3's idempotency check actually works, not just that it's present in the code. Separately, send a payload with a tampered `data.object` but the original (now-mismatched) signature, and confirm `verify_signature` returns `False` and the handler returns `401` before ever reading `event["type"]`. Finally, manually mark a completed batch as unprocessed (remove its `id` from `PROCESSED_EVENT_IDS`) and confirm `backfill_missed_batches` picks it up on its next run.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Checking `event["id"]` for duplicates *before* verifying the signature.** An attacker could replay a captured legitimate event's `id` in a forged payload — signature verification has to come first, always.
- **Doing the real processing synchronously inside the handler, then returning 200.** If `queue_batch_processing` is slow, the provider may time out waiting for a response and retry the delivery — which, without Step 3's idempotency check, would process the same batch twice.
- **Relying on pagination alone and skipping webhooks entirely**, assuming polling is "simpler." It technically works, but trades near-instant notification for a polling delay — exactly the tradeoff a batch-completion feature usually can't afford if users are waiting on a result.
- **Using an in-memory `set()` for `PROCESSED_EVENT_IDS` in a real deployment.** This example simplifies it for clarity, but a real handler needs a persistent store — an in-memory set is wiped on every restart, silently reopening the duplicate-processing risk Step 3 exists to close.
